scull.e: From Middle English sculle (“a type of oar”), of uncertain origin, possibly from North Germanic, from Old Norse skola (“to rinse, wash”).

d.g: One who sculls; an athlete who participates in sculling races.
d.x: The first and second guns had been fired, and the scullers in their boats, each some ten yards apart from the other, are anxiously waiting the firing of the third, which is the signal for starting.

d.g: A boat rowed by one person with two sculls, or short oars.
d.x: They watched that boat. It was a double sculler, with two female figures in the stern; it came slothfully up past the ferry; the sculling was not very good […]

sculler.e: English scull Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzijos Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English sculler From scull + -er.

d.g: a small room (in large old British houses) next to the kitchen;  where kitchen utensils are cleaned and kept and other rough household jobs are done

scullery.e: Inherited from Middle English squylerie, from Anglo-Norman squillerie (“office of the servant in charge of plates”), from escuele (“bowl, dish”), from Latin scutella.

d.g: present participle and gerund of scull
A servant from the lower classes.
d.x: They all looked directly at the ſcullion,—the ſcullion had juſt been ſcouring a fiſh-kettle.

d.g: Alternative form of macaroni.
A low, base person.
d.x: Away, you scullion! You rampallian! You fustilarian!

scullion.e: Either from Middle French escouillon (“a swab, cloth”), diminutive of escouve (“broom, twig”) from Latin scopa, or an alteration of Old French souillon (“scullion”) by influence of scullery.

d.g: A small fish of the family Cottidae, usually lacking scales. Often found on river bottoms and in tidal pools.
A person who makes mischief.

sculpin.e: From earlier scorpene, from Latin scorpaena, from Ancient Greek σκόρπαινα (skórpaina, “kind of fish”), diminutive of σκορπίος (skorpíos). Compare scorpionfish.

d.g: A person who sculpts; an artist who produces sculpture.
d.x: The feisty wife of a world-renowned Russian sculptor emasculated an armed thug outside her Soho home — saying he “didn’t have the cojones to shoot her,” police sources said yesterday.

sculptor.e: Borrowed from Latin sculptor, equivalent to sculpt + -or.

d.g: A female sculptor.
d.x: The opening of GALAS in Boston signifies the first organized presentation of lesbian-created art in this city. Over 60 photographers, painters, craftswomen, sculptresses, and performing artists are participating in this month-long celebration.

sculptress.e: English sculptor Late Latin -issader. Old French -essebor. Middle English -esse English -ess English sculptress From sculptor + -ess.

d.g: A three-dimensional work of art created by shaping malleable objects and letting them harden or by chipping away pieces from a rock (sculpting).
d.x: There, too, in living sculpture, might be seen / The mad affection of the Cretan queen.

d.g: More generally (since modernism), a three-dimensional work of art of any material or of mixed materials, whether sculpted, assembled, found, constructed or created using multiple techniques.
Works of art created by sculpting, as a group.
The three-dimensional ornamentation on the outer surface of a shell.

sculpture.e: From Middle English sculpture, from Old French sculpture, from Latin sculptūra (“sculpture”), from sculpō (“to cut out, to carve in stone”).

d.g: A sculptor.
d.x: Besides statues, the sculpturers and carvers of this period executed many figures, and even historical pieces, in basso and alto-relievo, as ornaments in churches, and objects of veneration.

d.g: A layer of impurities that accumulates at the surface of a liquid (especially molten metal or water).
d.x: During smelting, scum rises to the surface and is then removed by the smelter.

d.g: A greenish water vegetation (such as algae), usually found floating on the surface of ponds
d.x: These organisms form scum in large quantities.

d.g: The topmost liquid layer of a cesspool or septic tank.
Semen.
d.x: Horse, who was always talking about facts, said, “Man, that can't be scum, ’cause scum is white.”

d.g: A reprehensible person or persons.
d.x: People who sell used-up pens are scum, just total low-lives.

d.g: To startscum or savescum.

scum.e: From Middle English scum, scome, skum, skome, scumme, from Middle Low German or Middle Dutch schūme (“foam”), from Old Dutch *scūm, from Frankish *skūm, from Proto-Germanic *skūmaz (“froth, foam”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewH- (“to cover, conceal”). Cognate with Dutch schuim (“foam”), West Frisian skuum, German Schaum (“foam”), Danish and Swedish skum (“foam”). Compare also French écume (“scum”), Italian schiuma (“foam”), Saterland Frisian Skuum, Sicilian scuma (“foam”), Walloon schome (“scum, foam”), Lithuanian šamas (“catfish”) and skanus (“tasty”) from the same Germanic source. Related to skim.

d.g: An opaque kind of glaze (layer of paint).
To apply an opaque glaze to an area of a painting to make it softer or duller.
d.x: I want you to scumble the bottom third with sap green.

d.g: To apply a painted pattern to the finish of a piece of furniture to simulate the woodgrain of another timber, as for example to give pine an appearance of oak.
d.x: scumbled pine

scumble.e: Uncertain; perhaps from scum with frequentative -le.

d.g: To be sick of.
To dislike.
To cause to loathe, or feel disgust at.
d.x: But maybe she'd just got scunnered with Glasgow, fucked off to try her luck someplace else.

d.g: Dislike or aversion.
A young chav.

scunner.e: Borrowed from Scots scunner, skunner, from Old Scots skunnyr, skowner (“to shrink back; flinch”), from Middle English skoneren (“to feel sick or disgusted”), of uncertain origin. Perhaps from a frequentative of shun. If so, etymologically shun + -er (frequentative suffix). Compare also Middle English scurnen (“to flinch”), English scare, English scorn.

d.g: A common sparoid food fish, Stenotomus chrysops, of temperate regions of the Atlantic coast of North America; the porgy.
d.x: On a lark, he took a small scup, or porgy, and a stamp pad and demonstrated how to make a print.

d.g: A swing.

scup.e: Shortened form of Narragansett mishcùp (“porgy”) or its plural mishcùppaûog. The singular was also borrowed as mishcup, while another shortening of the plural yields the synonym paugie. The word was also borrowed as scuppaug.

d.g: A drainage hole on the deck of a ship.
A similar opening in a wall or parapet that allows water to drain from a roof.
d.x: I have said that our roof was decidedly Biblical in style; but to make it a dry one, something of a nautical character was added to its architecture, for on either side were scuppers, and it was slightly arched in the centre[.]

d.g: To thwart or destroy, especially something belonging or pertaining to another.
d.x: The bad media coverage scuppered his chances of being elected.

scupper.e: Uncertain. Perhaps from Middle English scope (“scoop”) or Dutch schop (“shovel”) + -er; or from Dutch scheppen (“to draw off”).

d.g: A large greenish-bronze grape native to the Southeastern United States, a variety of the muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia).
d.x: Plucking an occasional camellia, getting a squirt of hot milk from Miss Maudie Atkinson’s cow on a summer day, helping ourselves to someone’s scuppernongs was part of our ethical culture, but money was different.

d.g: A sweet, golden or amber-colored US wine made from this variety of grape.

scuppernong.e: Named after the Scuppernong River and Lake in North Carolina near which the grapes were first found and cultivated. Probably from an Algonquian word. Both senses, "grape" and "wine", are first found in documents from the 1800s-1820s.

d.g: A skin disease.
The flakes of skin that fall off as a result of a skin disease.
Any crust-like formations on the skin, or in general.
The foul remains of anything adherent.
d.x: The Scurf is worn away, of each committed Crime

d.g: A low, mean person.

scurf.e: From scurf (“skin disease causing scabs or scales; flakes of skin that fall off due to a skin disease, etc.”), from Old English scurf, from Proto-Germanic *skurf- (“to gnaw”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off, sever; to divide, separate”). Cognate with Dutch schurft, German Schorf, Danish skurv, Swedish skorv.

d.g: Something that is scurrilous.
To run with quick light steps, to scamper.
d.x: Then the piglet tore loose from the creepers and scurried into the undergrowth.

d.g: A dash.
Bustle.
d.x: "It is very pleasant here," replied Carrados tranquilly. "Very cool and restful with this armoured steel between us and the dust and scurry of the hot July afternoon above. I propose remaining here for a few minutes longer."

scurry.e: Perhaps from hurry-skurry, a reduplication of hurry.

d.g: A short, erect tail, as of a hare, rabbit, or deer.
d.x: Shakespeare's use of the word scut may be a sly reference to Mistress Ford's pudenda: see sense 3.

d.g: The buttocks or rump; also, the female pudenda, the vulva.
d.x: I rumpled her Feathers, and tickled her Scut, / And play'd the round Rubbers at two handed Put.

d.g: A contemptible person.
d.x: She didn't need a new dress! Me money! Me hard earned three hundred that I scraped and scrimped for. Me scut of a daughter puttin' it on her back in finery.

d.g: Distasteful work; drudgery
d.x: Let's devote mornings to the scut, do real work in the afternoon.

d.g: Some menial procedure left for a doctor or medical student to complete, sometimes for training purposes.
d.x: There's no question that it's sexist. [Female residents] are berated more on rounds, given more scut to do.

scut.e: From Middle English scut (“hare”); further etymology uncertain, possibly related to Middle English scut, scute (“short”), possibly from Old French escorter, escurter, or Latin excurtāre, scurtāre, from curtō (“to cut short, shorten”), from curtus (“short; shortened”) (from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”)) + -ō. A derivation from Old Norse skut, skutr (“stern of a boat”), or Icelandic skott (“animal's tail”) is thought to be unlikely. As to sense 3 (“the female pudenda, the vulva”), see the letter of 5 June 1875 from Joseph Crosby to Joseph Parker Norris published in One Touch of Shakespeare (1986).

d.g: A shield-like emblem or a small metal plate, both serving as protective or decorative elements.
d.x: The corpse lay in state, with all the pomp of scutcheons, wax lights, black hangings, and mutes.

d.g: A horny, chitinous, or bony external plate or scale, as on the shell of a turtle, the skin of crocodiles, or the feet and legs of birds.
d.x: Then one afternoon, as he's stripping the scutes and hide from a shortnose sturgeon, an idea hits him.

d.g: A proneural gene, often associated with achaete, that is required for the formation of many larval and adult sense organs
An old French gold coin.

scute.e: Borrowed from Latin scutum (“shield”). Compare scutum, escudo, scudo, and écu. Doublet of escutcheon.

d.g: an asterid dicot genus that includes the skullcaps
a genus of Scutigeridae
garden centipedes
a family of Chilopoda
A container like an open bucket (usually to hold and carry coal).
d.x: All through dinner—which was long, in consequence of such accidents as the dish of potatoes being mislaid in the coal skuttle and the handle of the corkscrew coming off and striking the young woman in the chin—Mrs. Jellyby preserved the evenness of her disposition.

d.g: A broad, shallow basket.
A small hatch or opening in a boat, sometimes one used for draining water from open deck.
A drained trough between the windscreen and bonnet of a motor vehicle, forming the intake to the heating/air-conditioning system, often also containing the windscreen wiper motor.

scuttle.e: From Middle English scuttel, scutel, from Old English scutel (“dish, platter”), from Latin scutella, diminutive form of Latin scutra (“flat tray, dish”), perhaps related to Latin scutum (“shield”); compare Dutch schotel and German Schüssel. Doublet of écuelle.

d.g: Originally (now chiefly historical), a cask with a hole cut into its top, used to provide drinking water on board a ship; now (by extension, informal), a drinking fountain on a modern ship.
d.x: [S]o they continue to fire as directed, until they are either sent down to the cock-pit themselves, or have a momentary respite from their exertions, when, choaked with smoke and gunpowder, they go aft to the scuttle-butt, to remove their parching thirst.

d.g: Gossip, idle chatter; also, rumour.
d.x: His resolve not to worry about unfounded scuttlebutt lasted about two minutes.

d.g: To spread (information) by way of gossip or rumour.
d.x: Despite my sister's story, I am pretty sure they would have dismissed the bride story as so much malarkey scuttlebutted about by the town "talkers."

d.g: To chat idly or gossip; also, to spread rumours.
d.x: During the fighting for Manila, it was scuttle-butted among the troops that they must never put pin-up pictures on the walls of the Manila Hotel because Mrs. [Douglas] MacArthur owned fifty per cent of the property and Brigadier General Courtney Whitney, of MacArthur's staff, owned the other half.

scuttlebutt.e: The noun is derived from scuttle (“to cut a hole through (something)”) + butt (“wooden cask”). Noun sense 2 (“gossip, idle chatter; rumour”) refers to the fact that sailors would gather around the scuttlebutt to drink and exchange gossip; compare furphy and water cooler. The verb is derived from the noun.

d.g: small bottom-dwelling sharks

(Greek mythology) a sea nymph transformed into a sea monster who lived on one side of a narrow strait;  drowned and devoured sailors who tried to escape Charybdis (a whirlpool) on the other side of the strait
A personification of said rock as a ravenous monster.
A princess, daughter of King Nisos of Megara, who fell in love with King Minos and betrayed her city to him.
d.x: Ah cease rash Youth! desist e'er 'tis too late, / Fear the just Gods, and think of Scylla′s Fate!

scylla.e: From Latin Scylla, from Ancient Greek Σκύλλα (Skúlla).

d.g: plural of scyphozoan
Any true jellyfish of the class Scyphozoa.
A kind of large drinking cup used in Ancient Greece and Ancient Rome, especially by poor people.
The cup of a narcissus, or a similar appendage to the corolla in other flowers.
A cup-shaped stem or podetium in lichens.

scyphus.e: Borrowed from Latin scyphus (“cup”), from Ancient Greek σκῠ́φος (skŭ́phos).

d.g: An instrument for mowing grass, grain, etc. by hand, composed of a long, curving blade with a sharp concave edge, fastened to a long handle called a snath.
d.x:
And nothing 'gainst Time's scythe can make defence
Save breed, to brave him when he takes thee hence.

d.g: A scythe-shaped blade attached to ancient war chariots.
The tenth Lenormand card.
To use a scythe.

scythe.e: From Middle English sythe, sithe, from Old English sīþe, sīgþe, sigdi (“sickle”), from Proto-West Germanic *sigiþi, from Proto-Germanic *sigiþiz, *sigiþō, derived from *seg- (“saw”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek- (“to cut”). Immediate Germanic cognates include Middle Low German sēgede, Dutch zicht, Icelandic sigð (all “sickle”). More distantly related with Dutch zeis, German Sense (both “scythe”). Also akin to English saw, which see. The silent c crept in during the early 15th century owing to folk-etymological association with Medieval Latin scissor (“tailor, carver”), from Latin scindō (“to cut, rend, split”). The verb, which was first used in the intransitive sense, is from the noun.

d.g: an ancient area of Eurasia extending from the Black Sea to the Aral Sea that was populated by Scythians from the eighth to the fourth century BC

scythia.e: Borrowed from Latin Scythia, from Ancient Greek Σκυθία (Skuthía).

d.g: Non-Oxford British English standard spelling of scandalize.
d.x: He never greatly cared for the society of what are called good people. If any of these were scandalised (and offences were sure to arise), he could not help it.

scandalise.e: English scandal English -ise English scandalise From scandal + -ise.

d.g: To cause great offense to (someone); to shock with something scandalous.
d.x: Overhearing the lewd joke, the dowager gave a scandalized gasp.

d.g: To reduce the area and efficiency of a sail by expedient means (e.g. slacking the peak and tricing up the tack) without properly reefing, thus slowing boat speed.
d.x: The mainsail was "scandalised" - a nautical mode of describing a sail reefed at both ends[.]

scandalize.e: From Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, scandal + -ize.

d.g: To remove thatch (build-up of organic matter on the soil) from a lawn, to dethatch.
To make scratches or cuts on.
d.x: A combing tool is used to scarify, cross-scratch, or score the surface of a scratch coat or undercoat of plaster.

d.g: To damage the testa (seed coat) of a seed by cutting, scraping, chemicals, hot water, or fire to allow permeation of water and faster germination.
To break up, loosen, or roughen the surface of a field or road or a hard surface.

scarify.e: From French scarifier, from Late Latin scarificāre, from Latin scarifāre (“to scarify”), from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai, “scratch”), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”). Unrelated to scar.

d.g: Chiefly in scarper the letty: to depart quickly or run away from (a place); to flee.
d.x: jean: We can't all spend our time nailing our suitcases to the floor, and shin out of the window. / archie: Scarper the letty.

d.g: To depart quickly; to escape, to flee, to run away.
d.x: A horse takes fright and "scarpers," or runs away.

d.g: Chiefly in do a scarper: an act of departing quickly or running away; an escape, a flight.
d.x: As a matter of fact we were all pritty flabergasted, for although we had all planned to do a scarper none of us realy thought we would have the guts to do it.

scarper.e: The verb is probably borrowed from Italian scappare (“to run away, escape, flee”), from Vulgar Latin *excappāre (“to escape”), from Latin ex- (prefix meaning ‘away; out’) + cappa (“(Late Latin) cape, cloak (usually with a hood); (Medieval Latin) cap; headwear”) (further etymology uncertain, probably ultimately from caput (“head”), from dialectal Proto-Indo-European *káput (“head”)) + -āre (the present active infinitive of -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs)). Around World War I (1914–1918), the English word was influenced by the Cockney rhyming slang term Scapa Flow (“to go”). Doublet of escape and scape. The noun is derived from the verb.

d.g: To collect and remove refuse, or to search through refuse, carrion, or abandoned items for useful material.
d.x: We scavenged a couple of old beer cans for our art project.

d.g: To remove unwanted material from something, especially to purify molten metal by removing impurities.
To expel the exhaust gases from the cylinder of an internal combustion engine, and draw in air for the next cycle.
To feed on carrion or refuse.
The rising motion of water as a wave passes; a surge; the upward angular displacement of a vessel, opposed to pitch, the correlative downward movement.
To heave upward.

scend.e: A corruption of send, influenced by ascend.

d.g: Alternative form of schematize.
To organize according to a scheme.
To distort and simplify for the purpose of highlighting certain characteristics.
To make a plan in outline.

schematize.e: Compare French schématiser, from Ancient Greek σχημᾰτίζω (skhēmătízō, “I assume a position”).

d.g: to scrounge, sponge, cadge
d.x: For quotations using this term, see Citations:schnorr.

schnorr.e: From Yiddish שנאָרן (shnorn), cf. German schnorren.

d.g: A straight run downhill.
d.x: The hand slid down the schuss of material and plucked at the hem.

d.g: To ski a schuss.
d.x: When, on his first time on skis, he just schussed down the mountain, we knew he was a natural.

d.g: To give off sparks; to shine as if emanating sparks; to twinkle or glow.
d.x: The streets of Rangoon, wallowing in sun, flashed and scintillated with strolling crowds, skirted in their best silk longyis.

d.g: Of a star or other celestial body: to vary rapidly in brightness; to twinkle.
Especially of a phosphor: to emit a flash of light upon absorbing ionizing radiation.
To dazzle or to impress.

scintillate.e: Borrowed from Latin scintillātus, past participle of scintillāre (“to sparkle, glitter, gleam, flash”), from scintilla (“a spark”). Doublet of tinsel.

d.g: Attributive form of scissors.
d.x: I had clipped out the photo, feeling pathetic about the act from the moment I slipped my thumb into the scissor hole.

d.g: One blade on a pair of scissors.
Scissors.
Used in certain noun phrases to denote a thing resembling the action of scissors, as scissor kick, scissor hold (wrestling), scissor jack.

scissor.e: From Middle English cysour, cysoure, cysowre, altered from sisours (“scissors”), from Old French cisoires, cisours, cisur, from Latin caedere (“to cut”); current spelling influenced by Latin scindere, scissus (“to split”).

d.g: A sideways shuffling or sliding motion.
d.x: Instinctively, he lifted the chair a fraction, and gave it a little scoot away from her.

d.g: A dollar.
To walk or travel fast; to go quickly.
To run away hastily; scram.
d.x: You'd better scoot before my mother gets home and sees that broken window!

d.g: A scooter.
d.x: When you meet with your club, park in front of the café or bar so the world can see your scoots.

scoot.e: Of uncertain origin. Perhaps from Old Norse skjóta (“to shoot”), or perhaps related to Middle English scottlynge (“moving one's feet quickly, scampering”, literally “scuttling”), see scuddle, scuttle.

d.g: To leave in a hurry; to go away.
d.x: What are you kids doing on my lawn? Scram!

d.g: A gun, firearm.
d.x:
Bad be say she don’t usually do this
In the trap with a stick, I do this
Get ’round there with a scram
I don’t give a damn

d.g: To shut down (a nuclear reactor or similar thing) due to an emergency.
d.x: Startup of reactor recirculating pump resulted in flux spike scraming plant.

scram.e: Probably either: * a clipping of scramble by apocope; or * from dialectal German schramm, the imperative singular form of schrammen (“to scratch, scrape”), from Late Middle High German schramm, schramme (“a graze, scratch”); further etymology unknown.

d.g: make a crushing noise

scranch.e: Compare Dutch schransen (“to eat greedily”), German schranzen. Compare crunch, scrunch.

d.g: Alternative form of scranch.
d.x: ‘Joe,’ said Mrs. Milford, scratching her head, and throwing her beaver upon the sofa; ‘go and fetch me three or four cabbage-stumps, and tell cook to pare them, and send them raw to me, I could scraunch a peck, I’m so dry—we had such a lot of nasty outlandish dishes.’

d.g: shriek; screech
d.x: She did not run against chairs nor move a stool so that the legs emitted a "screak" of agony, and she could sit still for an hour at a time if she had a book.

d.g: shriek; screech
d.x: They walk together in silence while behind them a freight train chuffs and screaks through the crossing.

d.g: A pinching miser; a niggard.
To make too small or short; to shortchange.
d.x: to scrimp the pattern of a coat

d.g: To limit or straiten; to put on short allowance.
d.x: For, as a general thing, the English merchant-ship scrimps her crew; but not so the English whaler.

d.g: To be frugal, whether to a reasonable and wise extent or to a miserly and unwise extent.
d.x: “Oh, Electra, jewel of women, darling of my heart, we are free at last, we roll in wealth, we need never scrimp again. It's a case for Veuve Cliquot!”

scrimp.e: From Scots scrimp (“meager”), from Middle Dutch or Middle Low German schrimpen (“to shrivel up, wrinkle”), from Old Dutch *scrimpan, from Frankish *skrimpan, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skrimpaną (“to shrink”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker- (“to cut off”), related to Old English sċrimman (“to shrink”) and sċrincan (“to shrivel up”). Doublet of shrink, shrimp, and shrim.

d.g: To shirk duty.

scrimshank.e: Unclear. One hypothesis is that it derives from (the noun scrimshanker, from) scrimp + swanker (old military slang for someone who works hard).

d.g: To hunt about, especially for something of nominal value; to scavenge or glean.
d.x: scrounge for food

d.g: To obtain something of moderate or inconsequential value from another.
d.x: As long as he's got someone who'll let him scrounge off them, he'll never settle down and get a full-time job.

d.g: Someone who scrounges; a scrounger.
An act of scrounging; a trip taken for the purpose of scrounging.
d.x: "Still, it's not much good sending you two off on a medical supplies scrounge. What about food and general stores? Suit you?"

scrounge.e: 1915, alteration of dialectal scrunge ("to search stealthily, rummage, pilfer") (1909), of uncertain origin, perhaps from dialectal scringe ("to pry about"); or perhaps related to scrouge, scrooge ("push, jostle") (1755, also Cockney slang for "a crowd"), probably suggestive of screw, squeeze. Popularized by the military in World War I.

d.g: To examine something with great care.
d.x: Because his opinions are all over the place, they find it easy to scrutinise them and lay them out;

d.g: To audit accounts etc in order to verify them.

scrutinise.e: English scrutiny English -ise English scrutinise From scrutiny + -ise.

d.g: To examine something with great care or detail, as to look for hidden or obscure flaws.
d.x: to scrutinize the conduct or motives of individuals

d.g: To audit accounts etc in order to verify them.
To magically or supernaturally look into or (as an entertainer) predict (the future), using crystal balls or other objects.
d.x: The fortune teller claimed she could scry [into] the future.

d.g: To use magical means to see or look into (something that is happening outside one's sight, e.g. inside a building or far away, or in the distant past, or future, etc).
d.x: Scrying spells can simply toggle the state of hidden objects to the revealed state, […]

scry.e: From Middle English scrien, scryen, a shortened form of Middle English ascrien, from Old French escrier (“to cry out”). Influenced by Middle English descrien (“to descry”).

d.g: To form by sculpture.
d.x: They sculpted a statue out of clay.

d.g: To work as a sculptor.
d.x:
What do you do?
-I used to box, but now I sculpt.

d.g: To carve out gradually.
d.x: Landforms sculpted by the wind.

d.g: A modification that can be applied to an object, like a texture, but changes the object's shape rather than its appearance.

sculpt.e: From French sculpter, from Latin sculpō (“to cut out, carve in stone”).

d.g: The product of two vectors computed as the sum of the corresponding elements of the vectors, or, equivalently, as the product of the magnitudes of the vectors and the cosine of the angle between their directions.

scalar product.e: Coined by William Kingdon Clifford in 1877 in his book Elements of Dynamic.
